subject: physics
title: Electromagnetic spectrum and polarisation
key_idea: Electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at c in free space. Their wavelengths run from radio waves to gamma rays. Only transverse waves can be plane-polarised, so polarisation is evidence that light is transverse.

blocks.text: Electromagnetic waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields. They need no medium, so they cross a vacuum.

items: All electromagnetic waves are transverse.
All travel at the same speed in free space: c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
All can be reflected, refracted, diffracted and polarised.
They differ in wavelength and frequency, so they differ in how they are produced, absorbed and used.
For every region v = fλ gives c = fλ, so a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency.

rows: Greater than about 10⁻¹ m (up to 10³ m and beyond)

items: Visible light is the range 400 nm to 700 nm. The eye detects violet at the short end and red at the long end.
Regions overlap at their edges; the boundaries are approximate.

diagram.prompt: Put these regions in order from the shortest wavelength to the longest.

items: All electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at c in free space.
Visible light runs from 400 nm to 700 nm; gamma rays are the shortest, radio the longest.

blocks.text: A transverse wave can oscillate in any direction at right angles to its travel. Polarisation restricts it to one direction.

items.meaning: A transverse wave in which the oscillations are all in one plane.
A transverse wave whose oscillations are in many planes at right angles to its travel.
A filter that lets through only the oscillations in one plane.

items: A polarising filter transmits only the component of the oscillation parallel to its transmission direction.
Two filters with transmission directions at right angles ('crossed') let no light through.
Rotating one of two filters in a beam changes the transmitted intensity. It falls from maximum to zero over 90° and is back at maximum after 180°.
Only transverse waves can be polarised. Sound cannot, because its oscillation is along its travel.
Polarisation is therefore evidence that light is a transverse wave.
Light reflected from water or glass is partly polarised, which is why polarising sunglasses reduce glare.
A metal grille polarises microwaves. A grille with its bars parallel to the electric field does not transmit the wave. Turned through 90°, it does.
Polaroid is a plastic that polarises light.
Plane-polarised means oscillating in one plane only.
Only transverse waves polarise, so polarisation shows that light is transverse.

checks.q: State two properties that all electromagnetic waves share.
checks.a: Any two of: they are transverse; they travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3.00 × 10⁸ m/s); they need no medium; they can be reflected, refracted, diffracted and polarised.

checks.q: Visible light has wavelengths from 400 nm to 700 nm. Calculate the frequency of light of wavelength 500 nm.
Explain why sound waves cannot be polarised but light can.
checks.a: Polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane at right angles to travel. Light is transverse so it can be restricted; sound is longitudinal and its oscillation is along the direction of travel, so there is no plane to restrict.

blocks.text: Malus's law gives the intensity of plane-polarised light after it passes through a polarising filter.

blocks.label: Malus's law
where: I₀ = intensity of the plane-polarised light entering the filter (W/m²)
θ = angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission direction of the filter

items: At θ = 0° all the intensity is transmitted. At θ = 90° none is transmitted.
For a series of filters, apply the law at each filter in turn, using the new plane of polarisation each time.
Calculating the effect of a filter on unpolarised light is not required.
Reflection, refraction, polarisation and diffraction can be shown with all waves, including water waves, sound, light and microwaves.
In a ripple tank, a flat dipper makes plane waves; barriers show reflection, a submerged block (shallower water) shows refraction and a gap shows diffraction.
Diffraction effects become significant when the wavelength is comparable to the gap width.
With microwaves, a metal grille between a transmitter and a receiver shows polarisation: the signal changes as the grille is rotated.
With light, rotate one polarising filter in front of another and watch the brightness change.
